what_its_for: Pegvisomant is used to treat a condition called acromegaly, which happens when your body makes too much growth hormone. This medicine helps block the effects of too much growth hormone and brings certain levels in your blood (called IGF-1) back to normal. It is usually used when other treatments like surgery or radiation have not worked well enough.
how_to_take: Pegvisomant comes as a powder that is mixed with water and given as a shot (injection) under your skin (subcutaneous injection). Your doctor or nurse will teach you how to mix and inject this medicine at home. Always use a new needle and syringe each time. Rotate (change) the spot where you inject to avoid skin irritation. Common injection sites include the stomach area, thighs, or upper arms. Never inject into skin that is red, bruised, or irritated.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your IGF-1 blood levels. A typical starting dose is 40 mg given as one injection under the skin (the very first dose is usually given by your healthcare provider). After that, most people take 10 mg once a day. Your doctor may increase your daily dose by 5 mg at a time, up to a maximum of 30 mg per day, until your IGF-1 levels are in the normal range. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If you do not remember until the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next scheduled dose as usual. Do not take two doses in one day to make up for a missed dose. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store unopened vials of pegvisomant in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze. Keep the medicine away from light. Once you mix the powder with the liquid (after reconstitution), use it right away — within 6 hours. Do not use the medicine if it looks cloudy, has particles floating in it, or if the color has changed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid injecting into the same spot every time to prevent skin problems such as lumps or thickened skin. Tell your doctor if you drink alcohol regularly, as alcohol can affect your liver and this medicine may also affect liver function. Do not start or stop any other medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements without talking to your doctor first, as some medicines can interact with pegvisomant. Avoid letting the medicine freeze or get too warm.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you have: yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice), dark-colored urine, severe stomach pain or nausea, unusual tiredness or fatigue (these could be signs of liver problems). Also call your doctor if you notice: signs of a low blood sugar reaction (shakiness, sweating, confusion, dizziness) especially if you have diabetes; pain, redness, swelling, or itching at the injection site that does not go away; symptoms of your acromegaly getting worse (such as increased hand or foot swelling, joint pain, or headaches); or any allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing.
when_it_works: You may not feel an immediate difference when you start this medicine. It usually takes several weeks to months before your IGF-1 blood levels return to a normal range and you begin to notice improvement in your symptoms, such as reduced swelling in your hands and feet, less joint pain, or improved energy. Your doctor will check your blood levels regularly (usually every 4 to 6 weeks at first) to make sure the medicine is working and the dose is right for you.
special_populations: Diabetes: This medicine can lower blood sugar levels in people with diabetes. Your diabetes medicines may need to be adjusted. Monitor your blood sugar closely and report any changes to your doctor. Liver problems: Your doctor will check your liver function before you start and regularly while you are taking this medicine. Tell your doctor if you have ever had liver disease. Children: This medicine is not currently approved for use in children. Older adults: Use with caution; your doctor will monitor you closely. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The safety of this medicine during pregnancy and breastfeeding is not well established, so your doctor will help weigh the risks and benefits.
